reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails
clinicalPearls: Subungual exostosis is a benign bony outgrowth arising from the dorsal aspect of the distal phalanx, most often on the great toe
It classically presents in adolescents and young adults as a firm, tender, slowly enlarging swelling that lifts or distorts the nail
Pain is common, particularly with pressure from footwear, and the overlying nail may be elevated or destroyed
A history of trauma or chronic irritation is frequently reported, and the lesion is not a true nail tumour but a bone lesion presenting through the nail
A lateral radiograph of the toe is the key investigation and shows a bony projection continuous with the phalanx, capped by fibrocartilage
It is benign but is often mistaken for a wart, pyogenic granuloma, or ingrowing toenail, delaying correct diagnosis
Definitive treatment is surgical excision of the bony outgrowth, and incomplete removal may be followed by recurrence
reference.pathophysiology: Subungual exostosis is an outgrowth of mature trabecular bone capped by fibrocartilage that projects from the dorsal surface of the distal phalanx, usually of the hallux, into the space beneath or beside the nail. It is generally regarded as a reactive proliferation, often linked to previous trauma or chronic irritation, rather than an inherited skeletal disorder, and it differs from a true osteochondroma in its cartilage cap and clinical setting. As the bony mass enlarges it pushes upward against the nail bed and plate, causing elevation, distortion, or partial destruction of the nail and producing pain when compressed by shoes.
additionalDifferentials: Viral wart (verruca) of the nail unit
Subungual osteochondroma or other bony lesion
additionalInvestigations: Lateral and oblique radiographs of the affected toe to demonstrate the bony outgrowth
Clinical inspection for nail elevation, distortion, or destruction
Onychoscopy to assess the surface and vascular pattern of the lesion
Histological examination of the excised specimen to confirm the diagnosis
Assessment for a history of trauma or chronic pressure
Consideration of cross-sectional imaging for atypical or recurrent lesions
redFlags: Rapid growth, ulceration, or bleeding raising concern for a malignant bone or soft-tissue lesion
Atypical radiographic features suggesting a more aggressive process
Recurrence after excision indicating incomplete removal
Persistent pain with destruction of the nail unit requiring surgical assessment
reference.prognosis: Subungual exostosis is benign and is cured by complete surgical excision, after which the nail usually regrows, although incomplete removal can lead to recurrence and some residual nail deformity may persist.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the lesion as a wart or pyogenic granuloma and treating it destructively without imaging
Omitting a radiograph, which is essential to reveal the bony origin
Incomplete excision of the bony base, leading to recurrence
Failing to send tissue for histology to exclude a malignant mimic
references: Baran and Dawber's Diseases of the Nails and their Management
management: Complete surgical excision of the bony outgrowth, including its fibrocartilage cap, is curative and the definitive treatment
Avulse or partially remove the overlying nail plate to access the lesion and curette the base to minimise recurrence
Confirm the diagnosis histologically on the excised specimen
Provide analgesia and advise roomy, pressure-relieving footwear for symptom control before and after surgery
Follow up for recurrence, which follows incomplete removal, counselling that the nail usually regrows though some deformity may persist
Refer for dermatological or podiatric surgery with a planning radiograph of the toe
